title: Teens and identity
hook: young Sikhs work out what Sikhi means to them
tomorrow: Gurveer wears his turban to school. someone laughs. now what?

segments.voice: Yesterday Gurveer tied his first full turban, a crown you put on yourself every morning: crowned. A day later, someone asked Simran whose crown it really is.

Long bus rides home from away games turn into honesty hour. Somewhere past the second exit, a teammate leans over the seat. She's not being mean. She really wants to know. You do the gurdwara thing, the prayers, the kara. But is that yours? Or is it just your parents'? For once, Simran doesn't have a fast comeback. She's leaving for college next year. The question has been sitting in her too, and two answers start talking in her head.
screen: `HONESTY HOUR ON THE BUS.` → `"IS IT YOURS, OR YOUR PARENTS'?"` → `TWO ANSWERS START TALKING.`

segments.voice: Both answers are real voices among Sikhs, so let each one speak. The first says: live it, and it becomes yours. On ang 305, Guru Ram Das describes the Guru's Sikh not by a feeling but by a day: in paraphrase, whoever calls themselves a Sikh of the Guru rises early, bathes, and meditates on the Name. The practice comes first, and understanding grows inside it, the way a language becomes yours by speaking it, long before you could explain its grammar. The kara on your wrist was given, but every morning you keep it is yours. The second says: ask, and then it becomes yours. A faith you never questioned is borrowed. Its best witness is a story tradition tells about young Nanak himself. At a ceremony to give him the sacred thread his family's custom expected, he asked what the thread was for. In Asa di Var, on ang 471, he describes the thread he would wear, in paraphrase: compassion its cotton, contentment its yarn, self-control its knot, truth its twist. He didn't throw out what he was given; he asked what it was pointing at. Simran hears both, and notices they aren't enemies. One keeps the practice. The other keeps asking why. Some young Sikhs lean one way, some the other, and some carry both for years.
screen: `LIVE IT, AND IT BECOMES YOURS.` · `ANG 305: THE SIKH'S DAY.` · `ASK, AND IT BECOMES YOURS.` · `ANG 471: THE THREAD OF COMPASSION.` · then, large: `THEIR OWN SIKHI.`

segments.voice: Write two short lines by hand. First: one thing you were given, by family, faith or place, that you still keep. Second: one question you're still asking about it. Then sit with both lines in front of you, without choosing between them.
Teens and identity. Young Sikhs working out whether, and how, Sikhi is their own.
Your line: their own sikhi. Some find it by keeping, some by asking, some by both. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Young Sikhs work out their own relationship to Sikhi through practice, questions, camps, kirtan and talks with family; some keep the forms first and grow into the meaning, others ask first and take on the forms later.

fork.setup: you're a teen who keeps every practice your family taught you. your cousin keeps asking why before doing anything. what's his best case?
options: a faith never questioned is borrowed; even young Nanak asked what the thread meant.
asking proves the practices don't matter, so he can skip them.
the Gurus taught that questions come only after amrit.
fork.reveal: that's the strongest version of the asking view. the keeping view's best case is ang 305: the Sikh is described by a day lived, and understanding grows inside it.
